title: A Loop That Holds Its Rate: Sleeping Until a Deadline, and What to Do When a Cycle Overruns

questions.question: A loop does 2 ms of work and then sleep_for(10 ms), meaning to run at 100 Hz. What rate does it run at?
options: 200 Hz
About 83 Hz, since each cycle takes the work plus the period, 12 ms
It depends on the operating system's tick
100 Hz, since it sleeps for the period
questions.explanation: Measured at 82.6 Hz on real threads. A cycle is work plus sleep. Simulated, the 100th cycle started at 1188 ms where 990 was wanted. The line looks right, which is why it ships.

questions.question: The repair is sleep_for(period - work), measured per cycle. Over 300 cycles of a 10 ms period, how far off is it?
options: Off by exactly the work time
Exact, since it accounts for the work
It fails to compile
About 105 to 110 us late per cycle, 1.1 percent slow
questions.explanation: Every sleep overshoots a little and nothing corrects it, so the error is added up. Measured 3032 ms against 3000. sleep_until a fixed grid was 3000.1 to 3000.3 ms, about 1 us per cycle, because the deadline is computed from the start and so the error of one cycle is gone by the next.

questions.question: A fixed grid of deadlines is hit by one 45 ms cycle in a 10 ms loop. What does a plain fixed deadline do next?
options: Stops the loop
Waits for the next full period
Doubles the period
Runs the missed cycles back to back with no sleep until it has caught up
questions.explanation: Measured 5 cycles started late, and a shortest interval of 2 ms. The total time came out right, 300.06 ms, and the spacing was lost. A controller sees several updates a couple of milliseconds apart, each with a dt far below the period, then silence.

questions.question: Work of 8, 14, 35, 2, 2 ms in a 10 ms loop with the Pacer. When did the cycles start, and how many slots were dropped?
options: 0, 10, 30, 70, 80 and 4 slots dropped
questions.explanation: One for the 14 ms cycle and three for the 35. Every start is on the grid, and the sleeping loop that adds a period after the work started them at 0, 18, 42, 87 and 99. The count is what tells you the loop was running below its rate.

questions.question: A cycle finishes at 40 ms and 1 ns when its slot was due at 40 ms. What does the Pacer do?
options: Sleeps 0 and runs at once
Rounds down and treats it as on time
Drops the whole slot and waits until 50 ms
Throws
questions.explanation: It never runs missed cycles in a burst. Late by any amount loses the slot, with the sleep 10 ms minus 1 ns. That is the price of never bursting, and it is written down so it is a decision and not a surprise.

questions.question: Why does the Pacer take the time as an argument instead of reading the clock itself?
options: A loop that reads the time itself cannot be tested without waiting, and one that is handed it can be tested in no time at all, with a stall of any length, which is lesson 03-05's idea
So it can be used on Windows
Reading the clock is slow
Because steady_clock is not available
questions.explanation: The whole suite is pure arithmetic: 100 cycles, a 45 ms stall, a clock that went backwards. None of it sleeps, and the answers are exact.
